name: llama.cpp is MIT: no patent grant, no copyleft, only requires preserving copyright notices
symptom: You want to use llama.cpp in a commercial product and need to understand the license terms. MIT is simpler than Apache 2.0 but has no patent grant.
root_cause: MIT license grants permission to use, copy, modify, merge, publish, distribute, sublicense, and/or sell copies of the software, with only one condition: preserve the copyright and permission notices. There is no patent grant (unlike Apache 2.0), no copyleft (unlike GPL), and no trademark grant.
workaround: If you use llama.cpp in a commercial product: (1) you can use, modify, and distribute freely, (2) you must include the MIT license and copyright notice, (3) you have no patent protection from contributors (if someone patents a llama.cpp technique, you have no license), (4) you can sublicense under any terms. MIT is the most permissive major license.
notes: Verified: llama.cpp's LICENSE file is the standard MIT text (21 lines, 1.05 KB), copyright 2023-2026 The ggml authors. The lack of a patent grant is the key difference from Apache 2.0. For most commercial users, this is irrelevant — but if you're in a patent-heavy field, it matters.
